81 Years Ago;
139 US Prisoners were burned alive / executed by the Japanese during the Palawan massacre on Palawan Island in the Philippines - December 14, 1944

On August 12, 1942, 300 US Prisoners, survivors from Bataan and/or Corregidor, were transported to Palawan Island to be used as slave labor in the construction of a Japanese airfield, a project that took two years. 

In August 1944, Captain Kojima messaged his superiors on what action to take regarding the Prisoners when US Forces landed. 
The reply from General Tominaga, 4th Army Commander, was “At the time of the enemy landing, if the POWs are harboring an enemy feeling, dispose of them at the appropriate time”.

In September 1944 half of the US Prisoners were transported to Manila leaving an estimated 150 on the island to be used for other construction projects.

On December 14, 1944, air raid sirens were activated and the remaining prisoners were herded by the Japanese guards into trenches connected to previously constructed air raid shelters. 
The Japanese then poured barrels of gasoline into the trenches and lit the trenches and the entrances to the air raid shelters on fire. Any prisoners who managed to escape the fires were gunned down. 

An estimated 24 prisoners dug their way out the back of the shelters and escaped, but the Japanese hunted them down and only 11 managed to reach Philippine Guerrilla Fighters under the command of Nazario Mayor, where they were eventually rescued by a PBY sent for them.

US Forces landed in February 1945 with the prison camp and massacre site being discovered in March, which US Command already knew about from the 11 survivors. 

Post-War, remains which were identified were repatriated per the wishes of their family, unidentified remains were buried in a group burial at Jefferson Barracks National Cemetery in St Louis County, Missouri. 

General Yamashita was charged with the Palawan massacre and other war crimes committed in the Philippines, he was hanged in 1946.
Lt Colonel Satoshi Oie was tried and found guilty of war crimes including the Palawan massacre and was executed by firing squad in 1948.

Ten other Japanese officers were either sentenced to death or prison terms for the Palawan massacre.
Those sentenced to death had their punishments commuted to a 30-year jail sentence by General MacArthur. 
On December 31, 1958, these officers still in prison were freed under a general amnesty for Japanese war crimes prisoners.

Pictures from NARA 
WWP-PD

I didn’t come across Gabriel Go through an official MMDA press release or a polished government feature. I noticed him through the unfiltered lens of vlogger Dada Koo—where traffic isn’t sanitized, angles aren’t flattering, and reality has nowhere to hide.

In Dada Coo’s videos, Metro Manila reveals itself as it truly is: messy, impatient, flooded, choking, and relentlessly alive. And somewhere in that chaos, Gabriel Go keeps showing up—not as a talking head, but as a worker. No grandstanding, no microphone, no rehearsed lines. Just presence. Just action.

While others are content to supervise from a distance, Gabriel is there in the heat, the rain, the noise—coordinating, correcting, clearing, adjusting in real time. Through Dada Coo’s camera, it becomes obvious that he understands traffic not as a spreadsheet problem, but as lived experience. You see it in how he listens to enforcers on the ground, how he reacts quickly when a plan doesn’t work, how he treats congestion as an urgent, solvable problem rather than an excuse.

What makes this even more compelling is that this wasn’t staged. Vloggers don’t edit in competence. They capture it—or they don’t. And repeatedly, across ordinary days and ordinary crises, Gabriel Go passes that test.

In an agency often defined by press conferences and personalities, Gabriel stands out precisely because he isn’t performing for the camera. Ironically, it took a camera—Dada Koo’s—to reveal that kind of quiet professionalism.

Sometimes, the most credible endorsements don’t come from officials or speeches. They come from someone walking the streets with a camera, showing you who actually shows up when Metro Manila needs order in the middle of chaos. And through that lens, a 'no-frills' man of action in the person of Gabriel Go emerges.  @MMDA

🌾 @pixels_online WEEKLY RECAP | Dec 07–13

📉 Price Action (Dec 7–14)

$PIXEL opened around $0.0106 on Dec 7 amid low volatility and trended downward throughout the week, closing near $0.0093 by Dec 14, marking a ~12% decline.

Daily trading volumes averaged $60–80M, with notable peaks between Dec 10–12, while market cap slid to around $29M.
Support held above $0.009, reflecting broader altcoin market caution rather than project-specific weakness.
--------------------------------------------------------

🌾 NFT Market Snapshot — Farm Land by Pixels (ETH + Ronin)

🌍 Farm Land NFTs recorded $13.44K in weekly volume, down 38.8%, with 33 traders participating.
📉 Sales activity slowed, though market cap inched up to $4.88M, and the floor price rose to $547.39.
💰 Average sale price declined to $659.34, showing reduced high-end activity despite floor stability.
-------------------------------

🐾 Pixels Pets — Ronin Network

🐶 Pixels Pets NFTs posted $1.31K in volume, down 17.7%, with 53 traders active.
📊 Market cap held steady at $66.34K, while the floor price stabilized near $14.87.
💸 Average prices fell to $31.56, signaling quieter speculative demand.
--------------------------------------------------------

🛡️ New Hearth Modifiers (Bountyfall)

🔥 Bountyfall introduced rotating Hearth Modifiers, adding fresh twists to each session.
⚙️ Modifiers adjusted gameplay dynamically, boosting deposits, weakening sabotage, raising Hearth health, and shifting Union balance as milestones were reached.
🕒 These Modifiers went live on Tuesday at 12:00 AM UTC, encouraging players to adapt strategies each cycle.
--------------------------------------------------------

🎉 Conference Highlights — YPS & Binance Blockchain Week

🎤 At YGG Play Summit, Luke’s fireside chat filled the theater, and the Popberry Pancake Eating Contest crowned Jihoz as champion.
💎 At Binance Blockchain Week, the Pixels booth featured exclusive merch, veggie plushies, and interactive games, drawing strong foot traffic.
👾 Pixels also brought the Neon Zone to life in Manila, blending IRL mini-games, themed drinks, prizes, and community energy.
--------------------------------------------------------

📊 AMA Recap — Key Takeaways

🛠️ The team confirmed a strong building phase, focusing on backend upgrades and new products like Stacked and Chubkins.
🌍 Growth plans shifted toward blending Web2 user acquisition with Web3 systems, targeting mass onboarding.
🐾 A major animal care overhaul was confirmed, larger than originally planned.
✨ Improving new-user experience, UI, and onboarding simplicity remained a top priority.
📱 Stacked was positioned as a core ecosystem hub, supporting staking, rewards, offers, and stronger bot resistance.
🤖 Bot prevention focused on smart reward systems, A/B testing, and offer-based incentives.
💎 $vPIXEL utility was set to expand, with future marketplace possibilities and broader staking integrations.
🎄 A low-key, recurring holiday event was confirmed, alongside continued Bountyfall and Dungeon integrations.
🔮 Long term, Pixels leaned into Web3 strengths like ownership and ecosystem design rather than competing directly with Web2 studios.

--------------------------------------------------------

⚡ Avrenim’s Birthday Energy Party

🎉 Avrenim’s Birthday Energy Party took place on Dec 10 at the Drunken Goose, with the celebration streamed live on Twitch.
-----------------------------

🎟️ Moku’s Champion Slot Winners

🏆 Winners from Wart’s Great Escape were announced and rewards were distributed.
🎉 BossBoppa and Guppy93Allan claimed the Champion Slots, with the community thanked for strong participation.
